newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: De Klerk seeks bias ruling on S.Africa truth panel.
newsitem.headline: De Klerk seeks bias ruling on S.Africa truth panel.

text.p: South Africa's white-led National Party said on Tuesday it would seek a High Court ruling of bias against Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC).

The new low in relations between the party that invented apartheid and the commission appointed to document the damage done by the policy of legislated racial segregation followed an National Party demand on June 2 for a public apology from Tutu.

"We will ask the high court for a ruling that Archbishop Tutu, the TRC and (Vice Chairman Alex) Boraine have demonstrated a clear and consistent bias against the National Party," the party's justice spokeswoman Shiela Camerer told Reuters.
She said the party was acting on the advice of lawyers following the rejection by the TRC's lawyers of an ultimatum demanding Boraine's resignation and a public apology from Tutu.

The row erupted after former president F.W. de Klerk made a second submission to the TRC on May 14 in which he denied responsibility for torture and assassinations committed by apartheid police in the name of white rule.

The atmosphere during de Klerk's testimony was in sharp contrast to the almost jovial tone during Deputy President Thabo Mbeki's testimony on human rights violations committed by the African National Congress in its war against white rule.
Mbeki admitted and apologised for killings, beatings and rapes committed by ANC guerrillas during 30 years in exile.

De Klerk apologised for the harm caused by the approved policies of the all-white government prior to 1994, but said police hit squads who targeted members of President Nelson Mandela's movement did so without his consent.

Boraine criticised de Klerk later for refusing to accept responsibility for the actions of his government and Tutu told a news conference that de Klerk's testimony had brought him to the brink of tears.
National Party lawyers told Tutu in a letter on June 2: "You are required to apologise unconditionally for your conduct at the press conference...
"Dr Boraine is required forthwith to resign as Vice-Chairperson of the commission and as a commissioner," the lawyers said.
The TRC has heard gruelling evidence of the torture, assault and murder of men, women and children by police and soldiers, mainly during the final decade of white rule.

The commission has received more than 7,000 applications, most of them from former agents of the white government, for immunity from prosecution for human rights violations committed in defence of apartheid or in opposition to it.

The commission is scheduled to continue working until December, when Tutu, Boraine and others are due to start work on a report that will document the abuses of apartheid and, if necessary, apportion blame.
Camerer said the law that created the TRC demands, however, that witnesses and applicants should be treated impartially until the final report is written.
